agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 is the superscription plus the opening line (KJV 24:0 and 24:1), so the verse carries both. I glossed לַֽיהוָה as 'to YHWH [belongs]': the lamed of possession, with no verb, as STEPBible has it.

מְלֹא is rendered 'its fullness' in the literal layer, 'all that fills it' in the dramatic. Rashi (Eretz Israel / other lands) and Radak (the temple mount) read the verse as a framing for the temple liturgy; I mention this only as a tradition, since the text itself has no such limit.

history.note: [consider] Keep the superscription plain in the dramatic layer ('A psalm of David.') and leave the liturgical setting to the commentary. (PS.24.1: "לְדָוִד מִזְמוֹר".)

agent_notes: The refrain answer changes from 'YHWH strong and mighty' (v. 8) to 'YHWH of hosts, he is the King of glory'. Radak and Meiri explain the omitted 'mighty in battle' because the ark no longer goes out to war; Ibn Ezra gives a different reason. I use these only as readings of the tradition.

עַל with 'seas' and 'rivers': I kept the plain 'upon' in the literal layer. Radak and Meiri read it as 'beside, near'; the cosmic reading (earth founded over the waters of the deep) is the more natural one in the Hebrew picture and is the one I used. The mention of Rashi's seven seas and four rivers is his Land-of-Israel reading and is flagged as such.

history.note: [consider] Attribute the Land-of-Israel reading to Rashi and the midrash Radak quotes, give Radak's and Meiri's 'beside the seas' as their own reading, and frame Yam/Nahar as a modern comparison rather than what ancient hearers heard. (Radak on Ps 24:2: "ובדרש ... זו ארץ ישראל" and "ופרוש על ימים ועל נהרות: סמוך לימים ונהרות"; Meiri: "ר״ל סמוך לים וסמוך לנהרות".)

agent_notes: Written נַפְשׁוֹ (Ketiv) / read נַפְשִׁי (Qere). The packet table shows נַפְשִׁי with no Q marker; the commentary of Radak and Meiri names both forms. I glossed the pointed form 'my life/self' and discussed the written form in a note. Five English versions all render 'his soul' (BBE 'his desire'); Hebrew has 'my', and I kept it in the literal layer. I translated 'nefesh' as 'self' in the dramatic layer, and give 'life, throat, desire' in the note.

STEPBible glosses נַפְשִׁי as 'desire'. I corrected the gloss to 'my self' (nefesh): in the idiom 'lift up the nefesh to' it is the person's longing, but the Qere 'my nefesh' makes God the speaker, which is why Rashi and Radak read the divine oath formula (Jer 51:14, Amos 6:8).

history.note: [consider] Say 'the same root' for Laban's deceit, or keep only Genesis 27:35 as the matching noun. (PS.24.4: "וְלֹא נִשְׁבַּע לְמִרְמָה".)

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the 2 Kings 5:15 reference now says what Radak says (Naaman urges Elisha 'take a blessing from your servant'), and Radak, Meiri and the Targum are cited only for 'take, receive' (Radak ישא = יקח; Meiri = יקבל; Targum יְקַבֵּל). The nasa' echo with verse 4 is credited to Ibn Ezra (the reward set against 'did not lift up my self'). The KJV 'receive' is no longer called a loss: it is a fair rendering of the sense and only hides the repeated verb.

STEPBible glosses מֵאֵת as 'from with'; I kept 'from with' in the literal layer to show the preposition's 'from beside', and glossed the pair 'from with'. The literal layer keeps 'lift up' even though YLT 'beareth away' and the commentators take it as 'take'; I cannot tell from the Hebrew alone whether the picture of carrying is meant, so the commentary says only that the verb is the same as in verse 4.

(Radak on Ps 24:5: "ישא יקח ... ברכה על דרך קח נא ברכה מאת עבדך (מלכים ב ה טו)"; Meiri: "ישא ברכה כמו יקבל"; Targum: "יְקַבֵּל בִּרְכָתָא".)

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: 'Jacob' is now read as the name of the seekers ('this is Jacob'), as Radak (with Ibn Ezra, Meiri, Metzudat David) has it, and 'your face' is God's, the poet turning to address him (Radak). The KJV/Webster 'O Jacob' vocative is mentioned as the different reading it is. The earlier claim that Radak takes a vocative is withdrawn. Both literal and dramatic layers now agree: 'those who seek your face — Jacob'.

Ibn Ezra says 'Jacob' means the seed of Jacob and that no one need supply 'God of' (as BBE does, 'God of Jacob'); he does not report others supplying it, and my earlier note saying so is withdrawn. The Ketiv דֹּרְשָׁו (singular suffix) against Qere דֹּרְשָׁיו (plural) is from Radak; the packet table gives the Qere and I glossed it. Malbim's reading (the generation is all at the rank of Jacob, who saw the ladder) is an alternative I mention in the commentary and leave unsourced beyond his name.

history.note: [should_fix] Correct the commentary and the יעקב note: Radak (with Ibn Ezra, Meiri, Metzudat David) takes 'your face' as God's and 'Jacob' as the name of the seekers, not a vocative; mention the KJV 'O Jacob' as a different reading. Make the dramatic layer agree with that (e.g. 'those who seek your face: this is Jacob'), or, if you keep a vocative, do not attribute it to Radak and resolve the clash with 'speak to him'. (Radak on Ps 24:6: "מבקשי פניך יעקב כנגד האל מדבר המשורר: הם הם שיבקשו פניך בבית המקדש, יעקב והם ישראל"; Ibn Ezra: "הם זרע יעקב"; Meiri: "ויעקב ר״ל כלל ישראל הם מבקשי פניך".)

agent_notes: עוֹלָם in 'doors of olam': I translate 'ancient/ageless' in the literal layer and 'everlasting' in the dramatic layer. Rashi, Radak and Meiri tie it to the temple as the permanent house after the ark's wanderings; the text itself says only 'doors of olam'.
The sources for the story of the doors sticking together (Rashi on Ps 24:7, citing 2 Chr 6:42) are in the packet; Radak points to the Talmud (Shabbat 30a, etc.) which I cite only through Radak.

history.note: [consider] Render Radak's distinction as 'sha'ar is the gate with threshold and posts, petakh the opening (the entrance itself)'. (Radak on Ps 24:7: "ופתח יקרא מה שנשאר מן השער מן הדלתות ולחוץ. ולכך נקרא פתח, שהוא נפתח תמיד".)

agent_notes: I kept the STEPBible gloss 'strong' for עִזּוּז and make no claim about how often the form occurs; Metzudat Zion ties it to oz, strength.

Reviewer request addressed: the literal layer now carries '[your heads]' after 'and lift up', matching the commentary and Ibn Ezra's paraphrase (ושאו פתחי עולם ראשיכם). Radak adds that the single 'heads' stands for two, in the manner of the language. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David also offer the second-house reading (the glory returning with the redeemer), which I report as theirs only.

The verb changes from niphal הִנָּשְׂאוּ (verse 7, locked) to qal וּשְׂאוּ here. I read this as the doors becoming the agents of the lifting; that is my own reading of the grammar, not a claim of the commentaries (they speak of repetition, כפל). The Targum has the 'gates of the Garden of Eden' here; I did not use it in the text and mention it in the commentary.
